title: Stay in touch and find your way
short: Family contact, emergency radio, ham radio, map and compass
intro: Ways to reach family and get official warnings when phones and internet are down or overloaded, what you need to know before using two-way radios, and how to find your way with a map and compass or signal for help. Many readings are from US agencies; local rules, emergency numbers and services differ.

choices.label: Phones or internet are down or overloaded
choices.hint: Calls won't connect, need to find family

read.label: Save calls for emergencies and use texts
read.note: A 2024 sheet from FEMA (the US federal emergency agency) notes phone systems are often down or busy after disasters and suggests text messages or social media to reach family.

read.label: After an earthquake: text rather than call
read.note: FEMA P-530: stay off the phone except for emergencies, use text messaging, and get in touch with your out-of-area contact.

read.label: Using your family communication plan
read.note: FEMA's Are You Ready? guide: the out-of-area contact, two ways to reach them, wallet cards and practising the plan.

choices.label: I need official warnings and news
choices.hint: Emergency alerts, battery or crank radio; the readings describe US systems

read.label: Weather alert radio and local alert sign-ups
read.note: FEMA fact sheet: what NOAA Weather Radio (from the US weather and oceans agency) broadcasts, SAME receivers (radios that sound only for alerts in your area), opt-in text alerts and reverse-911 systems (automatic warning calls to local phones).

read.label: How emergency alerts reach your phone
read.note: Wireless Emergency Alerts (the US alerts sent to mobile phones) need no sign-up; also Emergency Alert System (EAS) broadcasts on US radio and TV, and keeping spare batteries or chargers.

choices.label: Ham (amateur) radio — can I use it?
choices.hint: Licensing (every country has its own rules; these readings describe the US), getting started

read.label: Ham vs GMRS vs FRS: licensing and range
read.note: Overview from TACDA (The American Civil Defense Association): ham operators must pass a test and get a licence from the FCC (the US radio regulator); GMRS (a US walkie-talkie service) needs a licence too; FRS (US licence-free walkie-talkies) does not. Points to local clubs.

read.label: Beginner's guide to ham radio
read.note: The Prepared (2017 prepper site): radio types compared, the FCC licence and test, and starter equipment. Not an official source.

read.label: Using your licence for emergency service (ARRL)
read.note: How licensed hams join ARES (Amateur Radio Emergency Service, US volunteer emergency radio groups) and the emergency training courses of the ARRL (the US national amateur radio association).

choices.label: Talking with neighbours without phones
choices.hint: Licence-free walkie-talkies (FRS in the US, PMR446 in Europe), CB, neighbourhood radio plans

read.label: FRS and GMRS radios for neighbourhoods
read.note: ARES Manual (2015): licence rules, channel-number confusion between brands, alkaline battery backup and coverage testing. GMRS licence term stated here may be outdated.

read.label: Working with neighbours and CERT groups
read.note: How neighbourhood groups, CERT (US community volunteer responder training) teams and licensed hams can plan local communications together.

read.label: Meshtastic: text over a LoRa mesh
read.note: Getting-started page for low-power LoRa radios that pass text messages without mobile phone or internet service. Requires compatible hardware.

choices.label: Find my way with a map and compass
choices.hint: No GPS or phone, reading a topo map, taking a bearing

read.label: Finding your way with map and compass (USGS)
read.note: US Geological Survey (USGS) primer: map scale, symbols, bearings and why the compass points to magnetic, not true, north.

read.label: Finding direction from the sun and shadows
read.note: US Army ATP 3-50.21 (2018): using the sun and shadows to find north; following pages cover stars and other methods.

read.note: Army method for dead reckoning: sight a landmark on your bearing, close the compass, walk to it, repeat.

choices.label: Signal for help or rescue
choices.hint: Trapped, lost, need to be seen or heard

read.label: Trapped after an earthquake: text, bang, whistle
read.note: FEMA: send a text or bang on a pipe or wall, cover your mouth, and use a whistle instead of shouting.

read.label: Protect your airway and signal rescuers (CERT)
read.note: If trapped, bang on an object or blow a whistle; yelling is a last resort.

read.label: Army signalling techniques (historical FM 21-76)
read.note: 1992 Army manual, superseded: getting attention with fire, light, contrast and patterns. Military context; wilderness focus.

limits.text: Ham radio operators must pass a test and hold a licence; the source describes the US FCC licence classes (Technician, General or Extra).
In the US you need an FCC licence to communicate on ham radio (the article says the test can be prepared for in days).
In the US, FRS radios may be used without a licence, but transmitting on GMRS radios requires a licence.
FCC rules allow an amateur station in distress to use any means at its disposal to attract attention and get help (the rule as printed in the ARES manual).
A compass points to magnetic north, not true north; the difference varies by place and changes over time.
If trapped, shout only as a last resort — it can make you inhale dangerous dust; tap on a pipe or wall or use a whistle.
